reference.source: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing and Cardiac Arrhythmias / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of sinoatrial node function causing inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, chronotropic incompetence, and sinoatrial exit block, often presenting earlier in life than acquired degenerative sinus node disease
Loss-of-function variants in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A cause an autosomal recessive form that may also feature conduction disease and overlap with other sodium-channelopathies

Variants in HCN4, which encodes the pacemaker 'funny' current channel, cause an autosomal dominant form characterised by bradycardia and blunted heart-rate response, sometimes associated with left ventricular non-compaction
A bradycardia-tachycardia pattern is common, with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter alternating with symptomatic pauses
Symptoms include fatigue, exertional intolerance, dizziness, presyncope, and syncope; some patients are detected incidentally on ECG
Ambulatory monitoring is key to correlating symptoms with bradyarrhythmia, since resting ECG may be normal
Permanent pacing is the mainstay for symptomatic bradycardia, and anticoagulation decisions follow standard atrial fibrillation stroke-risk assessment
Family screening with ECG and consideration of genetic testing is warranted given the heritable basis
reference.pathophysiology: Familial sick sinus syndrome results from genetically determined impairment of impulse generation and propagation within the sinoatrial node. Loss-of-function variants in SCN5A reduce the cardiac sodium current needed for rapid depolarisation, slowing conduction and depressing nodal and perinodal function, often with recessive inheritance. Variants in HCN4 disturb the hyperpolarisation-activated pacemaker current that sets intrinsic heart rate, producing dominant bradycardia and impaired rate acceleration. The resulting sinus node dysfunction manifests as bradycardia, pauses, exit block, and chronotropic incompetence, frequently accompanied by atrial arrhythmias in a bradycardia-tachycardia pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Athletic training-related sinus bradycardia and vagotonia
Hypothyroidism or other metabolic causes of bradycardia
Atrioventricular conduction disease and other inherited arrhythmia syndromes
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG documenting sinus bradycardia, pauses, or sinoatrial block
Ambulatory Holter or extended/implantable loop monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm
Exercise testing to assess chronotropic competence
Echocardiography to evaluate for associated structural disease such as left ventricular non-compaction with HCN4 variants
Thyroid function and medication review to exclude reversible causes
Genetic testing of an inherited arrhythmia panel with cascade family screening
redFlags: Syncope or recurrent presyncope with documented pauses
Very long sinus pauses or high-grade sinoatrial or atrioventricular block
Bradycardia-tachycardia with thromboembolic risk from atrial fibrillation
Family history of sudden death or need for early pacing
Associated structural heart disease or additional channelopathy phenotype
reference.prognosis: With appropriate pacing for symptomatic bradycardia and management of associated atrial arrhythmias and stroke risk, symptomatic and functional outcomes are generally good; prognosis is influenced by any coexisting conduction disease or structural cardiomyopathy, particularly in SCN5A- and HCN4-related overlap phenotypes.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to another cause when resting ECG is normal and failing to arrange prolonged monitoring
Overlooking reversible contributors such as rate-limiting drugs or hypothyroidism before implanting a pacemaker
Missing associated atrial fibrillation and its stroke risk in the bradycardia-tachycardia phenotype
Not recognising the heritable pattern and omitting family screening
Failing to look for associated left ventricular non-compaction in HCN4-related disease
